title: Growing chive microgreens
subtitle: The mildest allium microgreen, cut at 14 to 21 days
excerpt: Chive microgreens grow as fine, hollow green shoots with the gentlest allium flavour of the microgreen range. The cycle is 14 to 21 days. Chive seed germinates less evenly than leek or onion; expect sparser coverage.
sourceNotes: UMass Extension microgreens guides (open-access). Cornell Cooperative Extension indoor growing material. Standard microgreen-growing practice synthesised from extension service material.

glossaryTerms.definition: Watering by setting the growing tray inside a second tray filled with water, allowing the growing medium to draw moisture up from below. Keeps the seedling surface dry and reduces mould and damping-off risk in microgreen trays.

A fungal condition where seedling stems collapse and rot at the soil surface. Caused by Pythium, Fusarium, and Rhizoctonia species in warm, wet, poorly-ventilated conditions. Common in overcrowded or overwatered microgreen trays.

content.text: Chive microgreens are fine, hollow green shoots with a gentle allium flavour. They take 14 to 21 days on a 25 cm indoor tray: sow, blackout for four to five days until the looped shoots straighten, then grow in light until the shoots are 8 to 10 cm tall. The flavour is the mildest of the allium microgreens and suits dishes where leek or onion microgreens would be too sharp.
Chive seed germinates less evenly than leek or onion, and coverage tends to be sparser. Sow more densely than you think necessary (30 to 40 g per 25 cm tray) to compensate for uneven germination.

Light: a bright south-facing windowsill in spring and summer. In winter, a grow light at 14 hours per day 15 to 20 cm above the tray is recommended. Chive microgreens in low light are notably pale and produce very thin shoots that lack the structural quality for culinary use.
Temperature: 18 to 22°C. Chive seed germinates poorly at temperatures below 15°C. A consistently warm room is more important than for brassica microgreens.

Day 0: sow. Pre-dampen seed compost and fill the tray to within 1 cm of the rim. Scatter chive seed at 30 to 40 g per 25 cm tray; the fine black seed is lighter and more angular than leek or onion seed. A salt-shaker motion from 20 cm above the surface distributes it most evenly. Press gently into contact with the medium.

Days 1 to 5: blackout. Cover with a second tray, lightly weighted. Chive germinates slowly; the blackout phase runs four to five days. Remove the cover when the majority of shoots are upright at 2 to 3 cm. Some will still be looped; this resolves within 24 hours of light.
Day 6 onward: light. Rotate the tray 180 degrees every two days.
daily: set the tray inside a second tray with 1 to 2 cm of water and let the medium draw it up. Remove excess water after 30 minutes.
Days 14 to 21: cut. When shoots are 8 to 10 cm tall and a consistent green, cut 1 cm above the medium surface. Use fresh or refrigerate for up to two days.

attrs.heading: Troubleshooting
attrs.intro: Common problems on chive microgreen trays.

items.symptom: Very sparse coverage even after day 7
items.cause: Chive seed has lower and more variable germination than other allium microgreen seeds.
items.fix: Sow more densely on the next attempt: 35 to 40 g per tray instead of 20 to 25 g. Use fresh seed from the current season.

items.cause: Extended growing period in a warm, still room.
items.fix: Bottom-water only and ensure airflow. The mould is on the substrate; the shoots are safe to cut.

items.symptom: Shoots fail to green up after moving to light
items.cause: Insufficient light or room too cold.
items.fix: Add a grow light. Warm the room above 18°C.

content.text: Chive seed has a shorter viable window than brassica seed; use seed from the current or previous season. Standard vegetable chive seed is usually untreated. Microgreen suppliers stock chive seed in pack sizes suitable for tray growing.
is a concern over the long growing window. Bottom-water only and maintain airflow throughout the two to three week growing period.
